::: callout-note
## In this session you will learn to

1.  Chain steps together with the pipe `%>%`
2.  Standardize column names with `clean_names()` and rename columns with `rename()`
3.  Fix column types (dates, numbers) with `mutate()`
4.  Fix values with `if_else()` and `case_when()`
5.  Create new variables (BMI, age groups)
6.  Combine every cleaning step into one pipeline and save the result

**Before you start:** open the workshop folder in Positron (**File → Open Folder...**) and open `student_scripts/Session 2 - Cleaning_STUDENT.R`. Today starts from the raw files, `raw_data/linelist_raw.xlsx` and `raw_data/measles_raw.csv`, and works through the problem lists you wrote at the end of [Session 1](01-r-basics-importing-inspecting.qmd). If you fall behind, ready-made copies of today's results (`linelist_clean.rds` and `measles_clean.rds`) are in `processed_data/`.
:::

**Where this session fits.** Today covers **Clean** and **Save and share** (highlighted): you fix the problems you found in Session 1, then save the clean data so the next session can start from it.

1.  [Import]{.step}

You will build **two** cleaned datasets side by side: `linelist_clean` in the Follow along code, and `measles_clean` in the TRY ITs.

# Part 1: Set up and recall the problem list

Every session starts the same way: open the project, load packages, import data.

::: follow-along
**👀 Follow along 1.1** — Load today's packages: tidyverse, here, rio, janitor, and skimr.
:::

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(tidyverse)
library(here)
library(rio)
library(janitor)
library(skimr)
```
:::


::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## 🔍 What this code does

-   The same packages as in Session 1. Today `janitor` gives you `clean_names()`, and the tidyverse gives you the pipe, `mutate()`, `if_else()`, `case_when()`, and the `str_` text functions.
-   On this page the start-up messages are hidden; in Positron you'll see them in the Console. Messages are fine: only a line that starts with **Error** is a problem.
:::

::: follow-along
**👀 Follow along 1.2** — Import `raw_data/linelist_raw.xlsx` (`linelist_raw`) and `raw_data/hosp_info.txt` (`hosp_info`).
:::

::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
linelist_raw <- import(here("raw_data", "linelist_raw.xlsx"))
hosp_info    <- import(here("raw_data", "hosp_info.txt"))
```
:::


::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## 🔍 What this code does

-   Both files are imported fresh from `raw_data/`, the same way you imported data in Session 1. Today you clean a **copy** in R; the files themselves never change.
-   `hosp_info` is a small look-up table: one row for each of the 6 hospitals, with its correct name. You'll use it in Part 6 to fix the misspelled hospital names.
-   The extra spaces before `<-` only line the two lines up so they're easier to read. R ignores them.
:::

The problem list from Session 1 is today's to-do list:

| \# | Problem                                                            | Fixed in |
|----|--------------------------------------------------------------------|----------|
| 1  | Column names have spaces, dots, and capitals                       | Part 3   |
| 2  | Date columns are different types                                   | Part 4   |
| 3  | `age` is text, and 37 ages are in months                           | Parts 4–5 |
| 4  | Hospital names are misspelled or inconsistent                      | Part 6   |
| 5  | Gender and outcome have missing values                             | Session 3 |
| 6  | Impossible weights and heights                                     | Parts 5, 7 |
| 7  | 130 rows have no Case ID                                           | Session 3 |
| 8  | Duplicate rows? Not checked yet                                    | Session 3 |

::: callout-important
## Never edit the raw data file

All fixes happen in code. The raw file stays exactly as it arrived, so anyone can re-run your script and get the same result.
:::

# Part 2: The pipe `%>%`, `filter()`, and `arrange()`

In Session 1 you used one function at a time, with the data first: `count(linelist_raw, age_unit)`. Real work needs several steps in a row. The **pipe** `%>%` passes the data from one step to the next, **in order, from left to right**. Read it as **"and then"**.

::: follow-along
**👀 Follow along 2.1** — `count()` with the pipe, then sort by weight and show 3 rows.

Pattern: `DATA %>% STEP_1() %>% STEP_2()`
:::


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
linelist_raw %>% count(age_unit)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
  age_unit    n
1   months   37
2    years 6567
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
linelist_raw %>% arrange(wt_kg) %>% head(3)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
  Case ID infection date date.onset  hosp date date of outcome OUTCOME Gender
1  6056ba           <NA> 2014-10-20 2014-10-21      2014-11-05   Death      f
2  6056ba           <NA> 2012-10-20 2012-10-21      2012-11-05   Death      f
3  7400b3     2014-10-07 2014-10-12 2014-10-13      2014-10-18   Death      f
                 hospital age age_unit wt_kg ht_cm
1                    <NA>   0    years   -11    24
2              HMO Health   0    years   -11    24
3 Regional Medical Center   0    years   -10    13
```


:::
:::


::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## 🔍 What this code does

-   `linelist_raw %>% count(age_unit)` is the same as `count(linelist_raw, age_unit)` from Session 1. The pipe fills in the data as the **first argument**, so you don't write it inside the brackets.
-   `linelist_raw %>% arrange(wt_kg) %>% head(3)` reads: take `linelist_raw`, **and then** sort it by weight (smallest first), **and then** show the first 3 rows.
-   The first two rows share the Case ID 6056ba and both have a weight of -11 kg: an impossible value, and an ID that appears twice. You fix the weights in Part 5; repeated IDs and duplicates come up in Session 3.
:::

-   Keyboard shortcut for `%>%`: **Shift + Cmd + M** (Mac) or **Shift + Ctrl + M** (Windows)

## Keeping rows: `filter()`. Sorting rows: `arrange()`

-   `filter()` keeps the **rows** that meet a condition
-   `arrange()` sorts the rows; `desc()` sorts largest first

::: follow-along
**👀 Follow along 2.2** — How many patients have ages in months? Then the 3 tallest patients.

Pattern: `DATA %>% filter(CONDITION)`
:::


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
linelist_raw %>% filter(age_unit == "months") %>% nrow()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 37
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
linelist_raw %>% arrange(desc(ht_cm)) %>% head(3)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
  Case ID infection date date.onset  hosp date date of outcome OUTCOME Gender
1  ebb14f     2014-08-19 2014-09-01 2014-09-07      2014-09-13 Recover      m
2  610c15           <NA> 2015-02-04 2015-02-06      2015-02-20    <NA>      m
3  0b32d8     2015-01-07 2015-01-13 2015-01-14      2015-01-15   Death      m
                            hospital age age_unit wt_kg ht_cm
1 St. Marks Maternity Hopital (SMMH)  84    years   111   295
2                  Military Hospital  69    years   105   287
3                  Military Hospital  72    years    94   272
```


:::
:::


::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## 🔍 What this code does

-   `filter(age_unit == "months")` keeps only the rows where `age_unit` is exactly "months". `==` asks "is it equal?" for every row, and `filter()` keeps the rows where the answer is TRUE. `nrow()` then counts them: 37.
-   `arrange(desc(ht_cm))` sorts by height, tallest first. The top heights, 295, 287, and 272 cm, are impossible. They're on the problem list.
-   None of this changes `linelist_raw`. To keep a result, save it with `<-`.
:::

::: callout-note
## Conditions you can use in `filter()`

`==` equal · `!=` not equal · `>` `<` `>=` `<=` · `%in% c(...)` one of several values · `is.na()` missing · `&` and · `|` or

Use `==` (two equals signs) to compare. One `=` is for naming arguments.
:::

## Longer pipelines

Put each step on its own line, with the `%>%` at the **end** of the line. `select()` keeps only the **columns** you name:

::: follow-along
**👀 Follow along 2.3** — A longer pipeline, one step per line: `select()` `Case ID`, `wt_kg`, and `ht_cm`, then `arrange()` by `wt_kg`, then `head(5)`.
:::


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
linelist_raw %>%
  select(`Case ID`, wt_kg, ht_cm) %>%   # keep three columns
  arrange(wt_kg) %>%                    # sort by weight
  head(5)                               # show the first 5 rows
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
  Case ID wt_kg ht_cm
1  6056ba   -11    24
2  6056ba   -11    24
3  7400b3   -10    13
4  0fde59   -10    18
5  fca629    -9    24
```


:::
:::


::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## 🔍 What this code does

-   `` select(`Case ID`, wt_kg, ht_cm) `` keeps only these three columns, in this order. `Case ID` has a space in it, so it needs backticks.
-   `arrange(wt_kg)` sorts the rows by weight, smallest first, and `head(5)` keeps the first 5.
-   Each line ends with `%>%`, so R knows the next line continues the same pipeline. The text after `#` is a comment for people; R ignores it.
-   Without the pipe, you'd have to put each function inside the next one: `head(arrange(select(linelist_raw, ...), wt_kg), 5)`, which you read from the inside out. The pipe keeps the steps in the order they happen.
:::

::: callout-note
You may also see `|>`, the pipe built into R itself. For this workshop they do the same thing.
:::

::: callout-warning
## Common mistakes

-   Put `%>%` at the **end** of a line, not at the start of the next one. R stops at a complete line, so a line starting with `%>%` gives an error.
-   Don't end the last line with `%>%`: R then waits for another step (a `+` appears in the Console). Press **Esc** and remove it.
:::

::: {.callout-important .tryit icon=false}


```
3     MS-0908    104.0
4     MS-0523    104.0
5     MS-0132    103.5
```

```{.r .cell-code}
measles_raw %>% filter(`Temp (C)` > 45) %>% nrow()

```

:::


These are the Fahrenheit temperatures you found with `skim()` in Session 1: 27 of them. You'll convert them in Part 5. From here on, almost every piece of code in the workshop uses the pipe.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## 📖 Good to know

-   Most tidyverse functions take the data as their **first** argument. That's what makes the pipe work: whatever comes out of one step goes straight into the first argument of the next.
-   The pipe `%>%` comes from the magrittr package, which the tidyverse loads for you.
:::

# Part 3: Column names

## `clean_names()`

One function (from janitor) makes every name lower case, replaces spaces and dots with `_`, and removes symbols. `"Case ID"` becomes `case_id` — after this, you never need backticks again!

::: follow-along
**👀 Follow along 3.1** — Create `linelist_clean` from `linelist_raw` with `clean_names()`. Compare `names()` before and after.

Pattern: `NEW_DATA <- OLD_DATA %>% clean_names()`
:::


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
names(linelist_raw)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
 [1] "Case ID"         "infection date"  "date.onset"      "hosp date"      
 [5] "date of outcome" "OUTCOME"         "Gender"          "hospital"       
 [9] "age"             "age_unit"        "wt_kg"           "ht_cm"          
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
linelist_clean <- linelist_raw %>%
  clean_names()

names(linelist_clean)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
 [1] "case_id"         "infection_date"  "date_onset"      "hosp_date"      
 [5] "date_of_outcome" "outcome"         "gender"          "hospital"       
 [9] "age"             "age_unit"        "wt_kg"           "ht_cm"          
```


:::
:::


::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## 🔍 What this code does

-   The first `names()` shows the 12 original names, as in Session 1.
-   `linelist_raw %>% clean_names()` makes a copy of the data with tidied names, and `linelist_clean <-` saves it as a **new** object. `linelist_raw` is unchanged.
-   The second `names()` shows the result: `"Case ID"` became `case_id`, `"date.onset"` became `date_onset`, and `"OUTCOME"` became `outcome`. Only the names change; the data in the columns stays the same.
:::

## `rename()`

`rename(new_name = old_name)` — the **new** name goes on the left.

::: follow-along
**👀 Follow along 3.2** — Rename `infection_date` → `date_of_infection`, `date_onset` → `onset_date`, and `hosp_date` → `hospital_date`.

Pattern: `DATA <- DATA %>% rename(NEW_NAME = OLD_NAME, NEW_NAME = OLD_NAME)`
:::


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
linelist_clean <- linelist_clean %>%
  rename(
    date_of_infection = infection_date,
    onset_date        = date_onset,
    hospital_date     = hosp_date
  )

names(linelist_clean)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
 [1] "case_id"           "date_of_infection" "onset_date"       
 [4] "hospital_date"     "date_of_outcome"   "outcome"          
 [7] "gender"            "hospital"          "age"              
[10] "age_unit"          "wt_kg"             "ht_cm"            
```


:::
:::


::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## 🔍 What this code does

-   `rename()` changes three names. In each pair, the **new** name is on the left of `=` and the current name on the right.
-   All other columns keep their names, and there are still 12 columns.
-   `linelist_clean <- linelist_clean %>% ...` takes the current version, changes it, and saves it back under the same name.
:::

::: callout-tip
## One step at a time

We build the clean data step by step. Each step takes the current version, changes one thing, and saves it back with `<-`:

`linelist_clean <- linelist_clean %>% STEP()`

If your object gets into a bad state, re-run from the first step (`linelist_clean <- linelist_raw %>% clean_names()`). In Part 8 we put all the steps into one pipeline.
:::

::: {.callout-important .tryit icon=false}
## ✏️ TRY IT 3 (2 min): clean the measles column names

Create `measles_clean` from `measles_raw` with `clean_names()`. What did `` `Temp (C)` `` and `` `Vaccinated?` `` turn into?

✅ **Check:** `names(measles_clean)` includes `"temp_c"` and `"vaccinated"`

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
## Show solution


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
measles_clean <- measles_raw %>%
  clean_names()

names(measles_clean)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
 [1] "patient_id"       "report_date"      "district"         "sex"             
 [5] "age_years"        "vaccinated"       "fever"            "rash"            
 [9] "temp_c"           "days_in_hospital" "outcome"         
```


:::
:::


`` `Temp (C)` `` became `temp_c` and `` `Vaccinated?` `` became `vaccinated`: the parentheses and the `?` are removed, and the space becomes `_`.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## 📖 Good to know

-   The names `clean_names()` makes are in **snake_case**: lower case, with words joined by `_`. Most R code uses this style, and you never need backticks for it.
-   `clean_names()` also makes repeated names unique (a second `a` becomes `a_2`) and puts an `x` in front of names that start with a number (`2020 cases` becomes `x2020_cases`), because R names can't start with a number.
:::

# Part 4: Fixing types with `mutate()`

`mutate()` creates a new column or overwrites an existing one: `mutate(column = what_to_put_in_it)`. Use the same name to overwrite a column; a new name to add one.

## Dates

`as.Date()` converts text or date-times to dates.

::: follow-along
**👀 Follow along 4.1** — Turn `date_of_infection`, `onset_date`, `hospital_date`, and `date_of_outcome` into dates with `as.Date()`.

Pattern: `DATA <- DATA %>% mutate(COLUMN = as.Date(COLUMN), COLUMN = as.Date(COLUMN))`
:::


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
linelist_clean <- linelist_clean %>%
  mutate(
    date_of_infection = as.Date(date_of_infection),
    onset_date        = as.Date(onset_date),
    hospital_date     = as.Date(hospital_date),
    date_of_outcome   = as.Date(date_of_outcome)
  )

linelist_clean %>% select(date_of_infection:date_of_outcome) %>% glimpse()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
Rows: 6,604
Columns: 4
$ date_of_infection <date> 2014-05-08, NA, NA, 2014-05-04, 2014-05-18, 2014-05…
$ onset_date        <date> 2014-05-13, 2014-05-13, 2014-05-16, 2014-05-18, 201…
$ hospital_date     <date> 2014-05-15, 2014-05-14, 2014-05-18, 2014-05-20, 201…
$ date_of_outcome   <date> NA, 2014-05-18, 2014-05-30, NA, 2014-05-29, 2014-05…
```


:::
:::


::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## 🔍 What this code does

-   Inside `mutate()`, each line `column = as.Date(column)` overwrites one column with a date version of itself. Four columns are converted in one `mutate()`, separated by commas.
-   `onset_date` was text (`"2014-05-13"`) and the other three were date-times from Excel. `as.Date()` turns both kinds into plain dates.
-   `select(date_of_infection:date_of_outcome)` uses `:` to pick every column from `date_of_infection` to `date_of_outcome`. `glimpse()` then shows that all four are now `<date>`.
-   Missing dates stay missing (`NA`).
:::

::: callout-note
## Dates written in other formats

`as.Date()` expects year-month-day (`"2014-05-13"`). For other formats, the **lubridate** package (part of the tidyverse) has functions named after the order: `dmy("13/05/2014")`, `mdy("05/13/2014")`, `ymd("2014-05-13")`.
:::

## Numbers stored as text

`as.numeric()` turns text like `"56"` into the number 56. Text that isn't a number (like `"unknown"`) becomes `NA`, and R warns you: *"NAs introduced by coercion"*. That warning is fine **if** you expected it.

::: follow-along
**👀 Follow along 4.2** — Turn `age` into a number with `as.numeric()`.
:::


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
linelist_clean <- linelist_clean %>%
  mutate(age = as.numeric(age))

class(linelist_clean$age)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "numeric"
```


:::
:::


::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## 🔍 What this code does

-   `mutate(age = as.numeric(age))` replaces the text column `age` with numbers.
-   `class()` tells you what kind of values a column holds: now `"numeric"`.
-   There's no warning here, because every filled-in age was a number written as text. The 100 ages that were already missing stay `NA`. In the measles data (TRY IT 4), "unknown" can't become a number, so you will see the warning there.
:::

::: callout-warning
## Common mistakes

-   Forgetting the `<-` at the start: the result prints in the Console but isn't saved.
:::

::: {.callout-important .tryit icon=false}
## ✏️ TRY IT 4 (3 min): fix the measles types

In `measles_clean`:

a)  make `report_date` a date with `as.Date()`
b)  make `age_years` a number with `as.numeric()`. Which values became `NA`?

✅ **Check:** `summary(measles_clean$age_years)` shows a maximum of 999. Suspicious!

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
## Show solution


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
measles_clean <- measles_clean %>%
  mutate(
    report_date = as.Date(report_date),
    age_years   = as.numeric(age_years)   # "unknown" becomes NA (the warning is expected)
  )

summary(measles_clean$age_years)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.    NA's 
   0.00    4.00    7.00   12.13   12.00  999.00      27 
```


:::
:::


The 27 `"unknown"` ages became `NA` — that is what the warning is about. A maximum age of 999 is not a real age; we fix it in the next part.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## 📖 Good to know

-   R stores a date as the number of days since 1 January 1970: 13 May 2014 is day 16203. That's what lets you subtract dates or sort them. You'll see these numbers in Part 5 when something goes wrong.
-   `as.Date()`, `as.numeric()`, and `as.character()` all follow the same pattern: `as.` plus the type you want.
:::

# Part 5: Fixing values with `if_else()`

`if_else(condition, value_if_TRUE, value_if_FALSE)` checks every row and fixes the values that meet one condition.

## Ages in months → years

"If the unit is months, divide by 12; otherwise keep the age."

::: follow-along
**👀 Follow along 5.1** — Create `age_years` (ages in months divided by 12).
:::


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
linelist_clean <- linelist_clean %>%
  mutate(age_years = if_else(age_unit == "months", age / 12, age))

linelist_clean %>%
  filter(age_unit == "months") %>%
  select(age, age_unit, age_years) %>%
  head()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
  age age_unit age_years
1  24   months 2.0000000
2  NA   months        NA
3   7   months 0.5833333
4   7   months 0.5833333
5  24   months 2.0000000
6  24   months 2.0000000
```


:::
:::


::: {.callout-tip icon=false}
## 🧩 Reading a function call

Most cleaning steps in this workshop have the same shape as the code you just ran:

`linelist_clean <- linelist_clean %>% mutate(age_years = if_else(age_unit == "months", age / 12, age))`

| Piece | What it is | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| `linelist_clean <-` | the object and the assignment arrow | saves the result back under the same name |
| `linelist_clean %>%` | the data and the pipe | passes the data into the next function |
| `mutate(...)` | a function from dplyr (tidyverse) | adds or changes a column |
| `age_years =` | a named argument of `mutate()` | the name of the new column |
| `if_else(...)` | a function used as the value of that column | works out a value for every row |
| `age_unit == "months"` | the first argument of `if_else()`: a condition | TRUE or FALSE for each row |
| `age / 12` | the second argument | used where the condition is TRUE |
| `age` | the third argument | used where the condition is FALSE |

R works it out from the inside out: for every row, `if_else()` checks the condition and picks `age / 12` or `age`; `mutate()` puts the results in the new column `age_years`; and `<-` saves the changed data as `linelist_clean`.
:::

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## 🔍 What this code does

-   `if_else()` checks every row: if `age_unit` is `"months"`, the new `age_years` is `age / 12`; otherwise it's `age`, unchanged.
-   The second pipeline only **checks** the result and isn't saved: it keeps the rows in months, shows three columns, and prints the first 6.
-   24 months became 2 years and 7 months became 0.58 years. One of these patients has no age (`NA`), and it stays `NA`: missing in, missing out.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
## 🤔 Think about it: what would have happened in later analyses if we had skipped this step?

A 6-month-old baby would be counted as 6 years old. All 37 ages recorded in months would be too old, which would shift the age groups and the average age.
:::

## Impossible values → missing

Weights of zero or below are impossible. Instead of deleting the whole row (and losing the patient's age, outcome, and dates), we replace only the bad value with `NA`.

::: follow-along
**👀 Follow along 5.2** — Replace weights of 0 or below with `NA`.
:::


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
linelist_clean <- linelist_clean %>%
  mutate(wt_kg = if_else(wt_kg <= 0, NA, wt_kg))

summary(linelist_clean$wt_kg)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.    NA's 
   1.00   41.00   55.00   52.99   66.00  111.00      34 
```


:::
:::


::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## 🔍 What this code does

-   `wt_kg <= 0` is TRUE for the 34 weights that are zero or below. For those, `if_else()` puts `NA`; every other weight is kept as it was.
-   `summary()` now shows a smallest weight of 1 kg and 34 `NA`s. The rows are still there, with all their other information.
:::

::: callout-note
## 🔁 The base R way: `ifelse()` (one letter shorter, one big difference)

Base R has `ifelse()`, and you will see it everywhere. It works the same way **until you use it on dates**. Say we want an "estimated onset" that uses the hospital date when the onset date is missing:

::: follow-along
**🔁 Follow along 5.3** — Estimated onset (`hospital_date` when `onset_date` is missing) with `if_else()` and with `ifelse()`. Compare the first 3 values.
:::


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
if_else(is.na(linelist_clean$onset_date), linelist_clean$hospital_date, linelist_clean$onset_date) %>% head(3)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "2014-05-13" "2014-05-13" "2014-05-16"
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
ifelse(is.na(linelist_clean$onset_date), linelist_clean$hospital_date, linelist_clean$onset_date) %>% head(3)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 16203 16203 16206
```


:::
:::


::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## 🔍 What this code does

-   `is.na(linelist_clean$onset_date)` is TRUE where the onset date is missing. Then the hospital date is used; otherwise the onset date.
-   This code runs outside `mutate()`, so each column is pulled out with `$`.
-   Both lines pick the same values. `if_else()` prints them as dates (`"2014-05-13"`); `ifelse()` prints `16203`, the same date as a number of days since 1 January 1970.
:::

`ifelse()` silently turned the dates into **numbers** (days since 1 January 1970). `if_else()` keeps the type, and gives an error instead of a surprise when the two values have different types. That strictness is why we use `if_else()` in this workshop.
:::

# Part 6: Recoding categories with `case_when()`

`case_when()` is `if_else()` for **many** conditions. R checks each line in order and uses the first one that is TRUE:

```
case_when(
  condition_1 ~ new_value_1,
  condition_2 ~ new_value_2,
  .default    = value_for_everything_else
)
```

# Part 7: Creating new variables

## BMI

`mutate()` can calculate a new column from other columns.

::: follow-along
**👀 Follow along 7.1** — Calculate `bmi`, then set BMIs below 10 or above 60 to `NA` (the next two code blocks).
:::


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
linelist_clean <- linelist_clean %>%
  mutate(bmi = round(wt_kg / (ht_cm / 100)^2, 1))

summary(linelist_clean$bmi)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.    NA's 
  10.90   24.60   32.10   48.09   49.88 1250.00      34 
```


:::
:::


::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
## 🤔 Think about it: a BMI of 1,250?

That is impossible: the heights and weights don't fit together. Set BMIs outside a plausible range (10–60) to `NA`.
:::


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
linelist_clean <- linelist_clean %>%
  mutate(bmi = if_else(bmi < 10 | bmi > 60, NA, bmi))

summary(linelist_clean$bmi)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max.    NA's 
  10.90   23.20   28.70   30.58   36.50   60.00    1382 
```


:::
:::


::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## 🔍 What this code does

-   BMI is weight in kg divided by height in metres, squared. `ht_cm / 100` turns centimetres into metres, `^2` squares it, and `round(..., 1)` keeps one decimal.
-   The first `summary()` shows a maximum BMI of 1250 and 34 `NA`s: the weights you set to `NA` in Part 5 give a missing BMI.
-   In the second block, `bmi < 10 | bmi > 60` is TRUE when the BMI is below 10 **or** above 60. Those 1348 values become `NA`, so 1382 BMIs are missing in total, and the rest lie between 10.9 and 60.
:::

About 1,400 BMIs are now `NA`, because many height and weight values in this teaching dataset are unrealistic. Setting only the bad value to `NA` (instead of filtering out those rows) keeps everything else we know about each patient.

```{.r .cell-code}
  mutate(age_cat = case_when(
    age_years < 18 ~ "Under 18",
    age_years < 30 ~ "18-29",
    age_years < 40 ~ "30-39",
    age_years < 50 ~ "40-49",
    age_years < 60 ~ "50-59",
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
   age_cat    n
1    18-29 1487
2    30-39  598
3    40-49  252
4    50-59   78
5    60-69   27
6    70-79    6
7      80+    1
8 Under 18 4055
9     <NA>  100
```


:::
:::


::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## 🔍 What this code does

-   Each line checks one upper limit. A patient aged 25 fails `age_years < 18`, passes `age_years < 30`, and gets "18-29". `case_when()` stops at the first TRUE line.
-   The last line, `age_years >= 80`, is written out in full so that missing ages match no line and stay `NA`.
-   `count(age_cat)` shows most patients are children: 4055 are under 18. The 100 patients with no age are `NA`.
:::

Because `case_when()` stops at the first TRUE line, `age_years < 30` only catches ages 18–29 (younger ages were already caught by the line above).

`count()` lists the groups in alphabetical order ("18-29" before "Under 18"). In Session 5 you will learn how to put them in a sensible order with factors.

::: callout-note
## 🔁 The base R way: `cut()`

Base R's `cut()` makes groups from numbers by giving the **break points**. `right = FALSE` means each group includes its lower limit (18 goes into "18-29"):

::: follow-along
**🔁 Follow along 7.3** — The same groups with `cut()`. Check with `table(useNA = "ifany")`.
:::


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
cut(linelist_clean$age_years,
    breaks = c(0, 18, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70, 80, Inf),
    labels = c("Under 18", "18-29", "30-39", "40-49", "50-59", "60-69", "70-79", "80+"),
    right  = FALSE) %>%
  table(useNA = "ifany")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
.
Under 18    18-29    30-39    40-49    50-59    60-69    70-79      80+ 
    4055     1487      598      252       78       27        6        1 
    <NA> 
     100 
```


:::
:::


::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## 🔍 What this code does

-   `breaks` gives the edges of the groups: 0, 18, 30, ... and `Inf` (infinity), so there's no upper limit for the last group.
-   `labels` names the 8 groups, in order. There is always one label fewer than there are breaks.
-   `right = FALSE` puts each break into the group **above** it, so 18 goes into "18-29".
-   The result is piped into `table(useNA = "ifany")`, which counts each group, including the missing ages.
:::

The same counts as `case_when()`, and already in the right order, because `cut()` returns a **factor** (Session 5). Forgetting `right = FALSE` is the classic mistake: then an 18-year-old lands in "Under 18".
:::

::: callout-warning
## Common mistakes

Ending with `TRUE ~ "80+"` (or `.default = "80+"`) puts every patient with a **missing** age into the 80+ group. Write the last condition out in full (`age_years >= 80 ~ "80+"`) so missing ages stay `NA`.
:::

# Part 8: One pipeline and saving your work

Here is every step as **one** pipeline. This is the version to keep in a real project: one block that goes from raw data to clean data, so anyone can re-run it and get exactly the same result.

::: follow-along
**👀 Follow along 8.1** — One pipeline from `linelist_raw` to `linelist_clean`.

Pattern: `linelist_clean <- linelist_raw %>% clean_names() %>% rename(...) %>% mutate(...)`
:::


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
linelist_clean <- linelist_raw %>%
  clean_names() %>%
  rename(
    date_of_infection = infection_date,
    onset_date        = date_onset,
    hospital_date     = hosp_date
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    # Types
    date_of_infection = as.Date(date_of_infection),
    onset_date        = as.Date(onset_date),
    hospital_date     = as.Date(hospital_date),
    date_of_outcome   = as.Date(date_of_outcome),
    age               = as.numeric(age),
    # Values
    age_years = if_else(age_unit == "months", age / 12, age),
    wt_kg     = if_else(wt_kg <= 0, NA, wt_kg),
    gender    = case_when(
      gender == "m" ~ "male",
      gender == "f" ~ "female"
    ),
    hospital_name = case_when(
      str_detect(hospital, "Central")           ~ "Central Hospital",
      str_detect(hospital, "Military|Mitylira") ~ "Military Hospital",
      str_detect(hospital, "Regional")          ~ "Regional Medical center",
      str_detect(hospital, "Mark")              ~ "St. Mark's Maternity Hospital",
      str_detect(hospital, "HMO")               ~ "HMO Health",
      str_detect(hospital, "Premier")           ~ "Premiere Health",
      .default = "Other/Unknown"
    ),
    # New variables
    bmi = round(wt_kg / (ht_cm / 100)^2, 1),
    bmi = if_else(bmi < 10 | bmi > 60, NA, bmi),
    age_cat = case_when(
      age_years < 18 ~ "Under 18",
      age_years < 30 ~ "18-29",
      age_years < 40 ~ "30-39",
      age_years < 50 ~ "40-49",
      age_years < 60 ~ "50-59",
      age_years < 70 ~ "60-69",
      age_years < 80 ~ "70-79",
      age_years >= 80 ~ "80+"
    )
  )

glimpse(linelist_clean)
```

# Key points

-   The pipe `%>%` means "and then": `data %>% step_1() %>% step_2()` reads in order, left to right.
-   **Never edit the raw data file** — every fix happens in code, so anyone can re-run it.
-   `clean_names()` fixes every column name at once; `rename(new = old)` changes one.
-   `mutate()` creates or overwrites columns; `as.Date()` and `as.numeric()` fix types.
-   `if_else()` fixes values that meet one condition; `case_when()` handles many, checked in order. Use `NA` to blank out impossible values instead of deleting rows.
-   `str_detect()` and `str_to_title()` catch misspellings and inconsistent capitals; check every recode with `count(old, new)`.
-   Keep **one pipeline** from raw to clean data, and save the result with `export()` as `.rds` in `processed_data/`.
